analysis.one_liner: Requires standardized resin-identification labels on plastic containers and preempts state bans on labeled plastics.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced in April 1990, never received a committee vote or floor vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every plastic container sold in the U.S. to carry a standardized label identifying the type of plastic resin it is made from, using a numbered triangular symbol, with a separate "DEGRADABLE" mark for degradable plastics. The goal was to make sorting and recycling easier and to steer manufacturers toward degradable plastics. But it also contained a preemption clause: once a container carried the federal label, no state or city could enforce its own plastic-labeling rules or ban that container outright.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to recycle gain clear, uniform information about what their containers are made of, and recycling operations gain a standard code that makes sorting by resin type far easier. Plastic container manufacturers gain protection from a patchwork of state rules — the bill would have wiped out state and local bans on any plastic container bearing the federal label. The EPA gains a new enforcement role, funded by whatever Congress appropriates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, recyclers, and plastic container makers

how_it_helps.text: It requires every plastic container of 8 ounces or more — including bottles and trash bags — to carry a label identifying its plastic resin type, so consumers and recyclers can tell materials apart and sort them for recycling.

The bill sets a uniform national symbol and numbering system for the most common plastics (PETE, HDPE, vinyl, LDPE, polypropylene, polystyrene) plus a code for degradable resins, replacing the absence of any national labeling standard.

It gives the EPA authority to enforce the labeling rules, with civil penalties up to $5,000 per offense and misdemeanor criminal penalties for knowing violations, and requires annual reports to Congress on compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Plastic container manufacturers would bear the cost of adding the resin labels to their products and face fines or misdemeanor charges for violations. Taxpayers would fund the EPA's regulatory, monitoring, and reporting work, with appropriations left open-ended. State and local governments would lose the power to ban labeled plastic containers or set their own labeling rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Plastic container makers, taxpayers, and state governments

drawbacks.text: The preemption clause would have voided state and local plastic bans: no state or city could enforce a ban on any plastic container that displayed the federal label, overriding tougher local anti-plastic measures with a weaker national floor.

The bill defines 'degradable' very loosely — any plastic that breaks down within five years qualifies — so a container could be marketed with a degradable label even though it would persist in a landfill for years, potentially misleading environmentally motivated consumers.

Enforcement would have been light: a civil penalty of at most $5,000 per violation and a one-year misdemeanor, with appropriations authorized at 'such sum as may be necessary' and no dedicated funding stream.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A resin-labeling standard is a genuinely useful, low-cost tool: uniform codes make recycling easier and give consumers honest information, and the bill's labeling scheme resembles the numbered code that sorting facilities need. But the bill quietly pairs that consumer benefit with preemption of state plastic bans, a significant giveaway to the plastics industry that would have overturned local anti-plastic laws, and the loose five-year 'degradable' definition risks a wave of greenwashed labeling. On balance it helps ordinary people more than it hurts them, but the preemption provision is a real cost, not a technicality.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died quietly when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Glenn introduced the bill on April 3, 1990, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
Four senators — three Democrats and one Republican — signed on as cosponsors, giving it small bipartisan support from the start.
No committee action, markup, hearing, or floor vote ever followed; the action history shows nothing after the initial referral, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastic container manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided a federal labeling mandate, its penalties, and the EPA's enforcement regime, while states that had plastic bans kept them because the preemption clause never took effect. Consumers and recyclers lost a uniform labeling standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plastic packaging makers; state bans survived

sides.party_line_note: Four senators cosponsored the bill — three Democrats and one Republican — and no votes were ever taken, so its partisan shape cannot be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed labeling costs, EPA monitoring, and fines on plastic container makers — but its preemption clause would have voided state and local bans on any federally labeled container, a major protection for their market access. In the end they got neither obligation nor preemption because the bill died.

Uniform resin-identification codes would have made sorting mixed plastic streams far cheaper and more reliable, the core practical benefit of the bill. Its loss left sorting standards to voluntary industry codes.

The bill would have barred states and cities from enforcing their own plastic-labeling rules or banning labeled plastic containers, stripping authority over waste policy from the level of government closest to local landfill problems.

The bill created a 'DEGRADABLE' label and code designed to encourage use of degradable resins, giving this emerging product category a marketing standard — though the loose five-year definition could let marginal products claim the label.
